group.title: Education and learning
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: All the subjects and topics that a school or course teaches.
examples: Coding is now part of the school {curriculum}.
wrong: The curriculum is the bell that rings at the end of a class.

words.meaning: A list of the topics and readings for one course.
examples: Check the {syllabus} to see what we cover next week.
wrong: The syllabus is the chair the teacher sits on.

words.meaning: The money students pay to be taught at a college or school.
examples: {Tuition} at private colleges keeps rising.
wrong: Tuition is the money the university pays students to attend.

words.meaning: A university student who has not yet earned a first degree.
examples: As an {undergraduate}, she studied biology.
wrong: He became an undergraduate after finishing his PhD.

words.meaning: A student studying for a higher degree after finishing a first one.
examples: Most {postgraduates} here are doing research.
wrong: A postgraduate is a child who has just started primary school.

words.meaning: A long piece of writing based on your own research, done for a degree.
examples: She spent a year writing her {dissertation} on river pollution.
wrong: His dissertation was a two-line note he wrote in five minutes.

words.meaning: The main idea or argument that a piece of writing tries to prove.
examples: The {thesis} of the essay is that cities need more trees.
wrong: Her thesis was a random fact that the essay never tried to support.

words.meaning: Using someone else’s words or ideas and pretending they are your own.
examples: Copying a website word for word is {plagiarism}.
wrong: Writing every sentence yourself and naming your sources is plagiarism.

words.meaning: The process of judging how well someone has learned or performed.
examples: The final {assessment} is a spoken test.
wrong: The assessment told the teacher nothing at all about the students’ level.

words.meaning: A natural ability to do something well or to learn it quickly.
examples: He showed an {aptitude} for languages from an early age.
wrong: She has a real aptitude for math, so she finds it impossible.

words.meaning: The ability to read and write.
examples: The program aims to improve adult {literacy}.
wrong: His literacy is excellent, but he cannot read a word.

words.meaning: The ability to understand and work with numbers.
examples: Basic {numeracy} helps you manage a budget.
wrong: Her numeracy is strong, so she can’t add two numbers.

words.meaning: An experienced person who gives advice and support to someone with less experience.
examples: My {mentor} helped me choose the right courses.
wrong: A mentor is someone who refuses to share any advice.

words.meaning: A period of training where you learn a trade by working with a skilled person.
examples: He did a three-year {apprenticeship} as an electrician.
wrong: During her apprenticeship she worked alone and learned nothing from anyone.

words.meaning: Teaching the practical skills needed for a particular job.
examples: She took a {vocational} course in plumbing.
wrong: The vocational program teaches only ancient poetry and no job skills.

words.meaning: Required by a rule, so you must do it.
examples: Math is {compulsory} until age sixteen.
wrong: The class is compulsory, so you can skip it if you like.

words.meaning: Connected with studying, schools and universities, rather than practical work.
examples: Her {academic} results were excellent this year.
wrong: Academic skills are only useful for fixing car engines.

words.meaning: All the teachers in a university or college, or one of its departments.
examples: The {faculty} voted to change the exam rules.
wrong: The faculty is made up of the first-year students, not the teachers.

words.meaning: A class where a small group of students discusses a topic with a teacher.
examples: We discussed the novel in Thursday’s {seminar}.
wrong: A seminar is a lecture where a thousand students listen in silence.

words.meaning: Work students do during a course that counts toward the final grade.
examples: Half the grade comes from {coursework}, not the exam.
wrong: Coursework is done after the course has ended and counts for nothing.

words.meaning: Done at school but outside normal lessons, like clubs and sports.
examples: She joined several {extracurricular} activities, including chess.
wrong: Math class is her favorite extracurricular activity during lessons.

words.meaning: A high level of skill in something, such as a language.
examples: The job needs {proficiency} in Spanish.
wrong: His proficiency in French means he knows only two words.

words.meaning: Learning things by repeating them until you remember them, without really understanding.
examples: Times tables are often taught by {rote learning}.
wrong: Rote learning means deeply understanding ideas without ever repeating them.

words.meaning: An adult who starts college or university later than most students.
examples: As a {mature student}, she began her degree at forty.
wrong: He was a mature student, so he started university straight after high school at eighteen.

words.meaning: Learning by actually doing something, not just reading or listening.
examples: The museum offers {hands-on} science workshops.
wrong: The hands-on class was only a lecture, and nobody touched anything.

words.meaning: Having learned a skill by yourself, without a teacher.
examples: He’s a {self-taught} guitarist.
wrong: She is self-taught, having studied piano with a teacher for ten years.

words.meaning: Having a natural talent or very high intelligence.
examples: The school runs classes for {gifted} children.
wrong: He’s a gifted painter, but he has no talent at all.

words.meaning: The ability to understand what you read or hear.
examples: The test checks your reading {comprehension}.
wrong: Her comprehension of the text was perfect, so she understood none of it.

words.meaning: To make less progress than others, or than you should.
examples: If you miss classes, you’ll {fall behind}.
wrong: He fell behind, so he was ahead of everyone in the class.

words.meaning: Studying from home, with lessons online or by mail instead of in a classroom.
examples: She got her degree through {distance learning}.
wrong: Distance learning means attending every class in person on campus.

words.meaning: A school where students live during the term.
examples: He was sent to a {boarding school} at age eleven.
wrong: At boarding school, students go home to their parents every afternoon.

words.meaning: The level a student has reached, or something they have achieved.
examples: The report compares student {attainment} across schools.
wrong: Their attainment was high, so they had achieved very little.

words.meaning: A year off between school and university, often used for travel or work.
examples: She spent her {gap year} volunteering abroad.
wrong: During his gap year he studied full-time at university.

words.meaning: To study a lot in a short time just before an exam.
examples: I {crammed} all night for the biology test.
wrong: He crammed for the exam by studying slowly over six months.

words.meaning: To do an exam or course again, usually after failing it.
examples: He has to {retake} the math exam in August.
wrong: She retook the test, so she only ever sat it once.

words.meaning: To understand something, especially something difficult.
examples: It took me weeks to {grasp} the basics of algebra.
wrong: I finally grasped the idea, so I still have no clue what it means.

words.meaning: People who used to study at a particular school or university.
examples: Many {alumni} return for the reunion each year.
wrong: The alumni are the children who will start school next year.

words.meaning: How fast someone gains a new skill; a steep one means a lot to pick up quickly.
examples: The new software has a steep {learning curve}.
wrong: The learning curve is the shape of the classroom wall.

words.meaning: To practice and improve a skill you have partly forgotten.
examples: I need to {brush up on} my French before the trip.
wrong: She brushed up on her Spanish by never using it again.

words.meaning: The skill of judging information and arguments carefully before believing them.
examples: Good teachers encourage {critical thinking}.
wrong: Critical thinking means accepting every claim without question.
